items.text: Release speed. Slow bowlers usually bowl 70–95 km/h; slower gives the spin more time to act.
How far above the horizontal the ball leaves the hand. More loop means more time in the air for dip and drift to build up.
Height of the hand at release — roughly the bowler's height plus a little.
Where the ball would reach the stumps if nothing moved it. Drift and turn carry it away from this line.

Revolutions per minute: full turns of the ball in a minute. An A-grade club leg-spinner was measured at 1,670–1,920 rpm; top professionals spin it harder. More revs mean more turn off the pitch — but the air's push from the spin (the Magnus force) stops growing above about 800 rpm.
How the revs are shared. 0° = all top-spin (dip). 90° = all side-spin, spinning around the line of flight (turn off the pitch). 180° = all back-spin (floats on).
Tilts the spin axis so part of the spin is around an upright axis, like a lattu standing on the floor. That part is pushed sideways by the air, so it drifts the ball.

How cleanly the seam spins. A scrambled, tumbling seam can't throw the air the same way on every turn, so the push from the spin (the Magnus force) comes and goes. (The size of this effect is a teaching estimate — it has not been measured.)
Wind-tunnel tests found an old, scuffed ball gets more push from its spin (Magnus lift) than a new one.

How much the pitch grips the ball — the friction that fights its sliding. Dry, dusty pitches grip and turn; damp or grassy ones let the ball skid on. A teaching range — real pitch friction varies too much to pin to one number.
How bouncy the pitch is: the share of its downward speed the ball keeps as it bounces up. Hard pitches bounce more. Grip and bounce are different things.
Release speed. It decides whether the thin skin of air round the ball stays smooth or churns up (the Reynolds number) — and so whether the ball swings normally, not at all, or in reverse.
Where the ball pitches, measured back from the batter's stumps. The simulator finds the release angle that lands it there. Fuller balls have longer in the air to swing.
Where the ball would reach the stumps if it didn't swing.
Height of the hand at release — roughly the bowler's height plus a little. The simulator then finds the release angle that lands the ball on your length.
The seam's angle to the line of flight. About 20° is best at tripping the air on the seam's side into churning. At 0° (bolt upright) the seam can't swing the ball — only a rough/smooth contrast can.

Spinning the ball backwards along the seam keeps the seam steady, like a spinning top. Swing grew with spin up to about 11 turns a second (rev/s) in wind-tunnel tests; much more lets the smooth side churn up too soon, and the swing fades.
How much the seam wobbles in flight. A wobbling seam can't keep tripping the air on the same side, so there is little steady swing.
A round-arm, slinging action tilts the backspin, so the air's push from the spin (the Magnus force) points partly sideways. Positive pushes the ball in towards the batter.
Wear roughens the surface, and a rough surface churns up the air round it at lower speeds. A teaching curve — real balls wear very differently.
How well the fielders polish one half. The other half is left to roughen.
How bouncy the pitch is: the share of its downward speed the ball keeps as it bounces up. Hard pitches bounce more.
Off the sweet spot along the bat
Distance from the middle of the pitch to the rope. The batter stands about 8.5 m behind that point.
The ball's speed as it reaches the bat, after pitching. Each extra 1 m/s of it adds only about 0.2 m/s to the hit — your own bat speed matters far more.
Set mostly by the bat's angle at impact. With air resistance the best angle is a little under 45°.
Straight back past the bowler, or round to leg or off. Changes the distance to the rope and how the wind meets the ball.
A clean lofted hit comes off with backspin, which gives the ball an upward push from the air (Magnus lift) and more carry.

The biggest angle between hips and shoulders, seen from above, during the downswing: the hips open towards the ball while the shoulders stay back. On its own it explained 38% of the differences in bat speed — more than any other movement.
How far the front (lead) elbow straightens during the downswing. Male range-hitters in one study averaged 30 ± 12°.
How far the wrists release through the downswing — the last crack of the whip.
How cleanly the hips, trunk, arms and bat fire in order, each peaking as the one before slows.
A firm front leg at impact gives the body something to rotate around. Seen in baseball hitters.
A higher backlift gives the bat a longer path to speed up — at the cost of time against pace.
A heavier bat has more mass behind the ball, but you swing it slower: twice the swing weight costs about 16% of swing speed. The two nearly cancel.
Across the blade from its middle. 2 cm costs about 6% of ball speed and twists the bat, sending the ball up to 10° off line.
The sweet spot is about 17.5 cm up from the toe. Within 4.5 cm of it, ball speed drops by under 6%.

The air's push on the ball depends on how fast the ball moves through the AIR, not over the ground. A headwind raises that speed, a tailwind lowers it, and a crosswind both pushes the ball sideways and changes the angle the air meets the seam and the spin at.
Warm air spreads out and gets thinner (less dense), so every push from the air is a little smaller. Air at 15 °C is about 4 % denser than at 25 °C.
The air thins with height: at about 1,700 m it is nearly a fifth less dense than at sea level.
Humid air is slightly LIGHTER than dry air — water vapour is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it replaces. Wind-tunnel tests found humidity does not change swing.

A big hit is a chain. Your body makes the bat fast, the bat passes speed to the ball, and the ball flies through the air until it comes down. You don't need any physics to follow it — these five ideas are enough to start, and each card adds one more.

Speed is how far something travels each second. Scientists measure it in metres per second (m/s). TV speed guns use kilometres per hour (km/h). To turn m/s into km/h, multiply by 3.6: 40 m/s is 144 km/h. Spin is counted in revolutions per minute (rpm) — full turns in one minute.

Isaac Newton worked out two rules for how things move. First: a ball keeps going in a straight line at a steady speed unless a force acts on it. Second: when a force does act, the ball speeds up, slows down or changes direction. Scientists call any of these an acceleration. The same push gives a light thing a bigger acceleration than a heavy one.

Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth. Drop a ball and it falls about 5 m in the first second, getting faster all the way. A hit ball is falling like this the whole time it flies, which is why it comes back down.

Air resistance, or drag, is the air pushing back on anything that moves through it. Put your hand out of a moving bus window and you feel it. Drag acts against the ball's motion, so a hit ball slows down all the way to the rope.
A hit leaves the bat at 40 m/s. How fast is that in km/h?
Launch speed and launch angle — everything else adjusts them.

A hit ball moves forwards and upwards at once. The upward part of its speed decides how long it stays up before gravity brings it down. The forward part decides how far it goes in that time. Hit it too flat and it lands quickly. Hit it too steeply and it goes high but not far.
Once the ball leaves the bat, two things set how far it goes: how fast it is launched and at what angle. Air, wind and spin then adjust the result.
With no air at all, the best angle is 45°: the perfect balance between time in the air and speed along the ground.
Real air bites harder the longer the ball is up, so the best angle drops — to about 42° in the Loughborough group's flight model.
In their range-hitting study, batters launched at 37.5° on average. They were probably giving up a few metres for less chance of skying a catch.
The fastest launch they recorded was 39.5 m/s (142 km/h), and the longest carry 103.5 m.
Why is 45° the best launch angle only when there's no air?
Drag slows the ball more the longer it stays up. A slightly flatter launch (about 42°) loses less to the air, so it carries further.
Bat speed is built from the ground up.

Anything moving carries energy of motion, called kinetic energy. Crack a whip and the energy from your arm travels down it. The thin tip is so light that the same energy makes it move incredibly fast. Your body passes speed along in the same way, from heavy parts to light ones.

A big hit doesn't come from the arms. It starts with the feet pushing into the ground. Then it passes up through the hips, the trunk, the shoulders and arms, the wrists and finally the bat — each part speeding up the next, like the crack of a whip.
Order matters. Each part should reach its top speed just as the one before it slows down. Fire them all at once and energy is wasted. Fire them in order and speed builds on its way to the bat.
Illustrative: the order the research describes, not measured timings. Slide the simulator's Sequencing control to watch the peaks bunch up.
The simulator's sequencing control is an estimate borrowed from golf and baseball research — it hasn't been measured in cricket hitting. Its chart shows the pattern, not measured timings.
What goes wrong if the hips, trunk, arms and bat all speed up at the same moment?
The speed doesn't build up. Each part should peak as the one before it slows, handing its speed on, like the crack of a whip.
The single best predictor of bat speed.

Pull back a gulel (catapult) and the rubber stores energy. Let go and it flings the stone. A stretched rubber band, a spring or a muscle all work the same way. Twisting your hips ahead of your shoulders stretches the muscles of your trunk, ready to snap back.
The X-factor is the angle between the hips and the shoulders, seen from above. The hips start turning towards the ball while the shoulders are still held back, stretching the trunk like a spring.
Seen from above at the moment of greatest separation. The bar is the study's own number: 0.134 m/s of bat speed for every degree.

Scientists measure many people and look for the formula that best fits all their results — like guessing someone's height from their shoe size. That best-fit formula is called a regression. If one measurement "explains 38%" of the differences between batters, a bit more than a third of why some swing faster lines up with it. The rest comes from other things.

In 3D motion capture of 20 batters — from club players to an England international — the biggest X-factor in the downswing explained more of the differences in bat speed than anything else: about 38% on its own.

Start at 17.6 m/s and add a little for every degree of each movement. The simulator's default batter has 35° of X-factor, 25° of elbow and 45° of wrist: 17.6 + 4.7 + 1.6 + 3.1 = 27.0 m/s, about 97 km/h at the toe of the bat.

Peploe et al. (2017): bat-toe speed in m/s from the X-factor (X), how far the front elbow straightens (E) and how far the wrists uncock (W), all in degrees. Together they explained 66% of the differences between batters.
Every extra 10° of separation is worth about 1.3 m/s of bat speed — and, from the same study, roughly 1.3 m/s more off the bat.
Using the formula, how much bat speed do 10 extra degrees of X-factor add?
The last links in the chain.

On a merry-go-round, the outer edge moves much faster than the middle, though the whole thing turns together. For anything turning, speed = how fast it turns × distance from the centre. So a longer lever — a straight arm plus a bat — gives a faster bat toe for the same turn of the body.

The starting angles are illustrative: the study measured how much each one CHANGES during the downswing (here the simulator's defaults, 25° and 45°). Both changes lengthen the reach from shoulder to toe.

Front-elbow extension: batters with faster bats straightened the front (lead) elbow more during the downswing. The male batters in one study extended it by 30 ± 12° on average. The ± 12° shows how much batters varied.
Wrist uncocking: keeping the wrists cocked, then releasing them through the downswing, adds the final whip to the bat.

In a study of 15 male and 15 female batters, every man extended the lead elbow. But 8 of the 15 women bent it instead — closer to a checked drive. Whether that comes from strength, bat weight, coaching or shorter boundaries is still unknown.
The simulator treats these as separate dials. In a real swing they are linked — changing one usually changes the others.
Why does straightening the front elbow speed up the bat?
It makes the lever from shoulder to bat toe longer. For the same turning speed, a point further from the centre moves faster.
Why your bat speed matters more than the bowler's pace.

Momentum is mass × speed: how hard something is to stop. A slow truck and a fast cricket ball can both have plenty. In a collision, momentum passes from one thing to the other. A bat is about 7 times heavier than the ball, so a fast bat has plenty to hand over.

Restitution is bounciness: the share of the speed that comes back after an impact. Drop a tennis ball and it bounces high. Drop a cricket ball on concrete and it bounces far less. A bouncier impact sends the ball off faster.

Each 1 m/s of bowling adds about 0.2 m/s to the hit, but each 1 m/s of bat speed adds about 1.2 m/s. A ball arriving at 25 m/s, met by a bat moving at 30 m/s, leaves at about 0.2 × 25 + 1.2 × 30 = 5 + 36 = 41 m/s — about 148 km/h.
q, the collision efficiency, is about 0.2 for a cricket bat. It depends on how bouncy the impact is and on how much of the bat's mass is behind the ball where it hits.
So an extra 1 m/s of bat speed adds about 1.2 m/s to the ball, but an extra 1 m/s of bowling adds only about 0.2 m/s. That's why the biggest hitters make their own pace.
The simulator's default hitter, middling a ball that arrives at 90 km/h.
Cricket balls are not very bouncy. Fired at a rigid wall at 60–80 mph (about 97–129 km/h), they rebound at about 0.42–0.47 of the speed they hit it at — and less the harder they hit.
Which adds more to the hit: the bowler bowling 5 m/s faster, or you swinging 5 m/s faster?
Swinging faster, by far: 5 × 1.2 = 6 m/s more off the bat, against only 5 × 0.2 = 1 m/s from the bowler.

Push a door near its hinges and it barely moves. Push at the handle and it swings easily. A force far from the turning point has a bigger turning effect, called torque. A ball that hits towards the edge of the bat pushes far from the middle of the blade, so it twists the bat in your hands.

The Loughborough group placed the sweet spot about 17.5 cm up from the toe, along the middle of the bat. Where the ball hit the bat explained 48% of the differences in ball speed — more than bat speed did on its own.
Zones from Peploe et al.'s measurements of how much speed each off-centre hit costs. The ring is a ball at true size, where the "Mistimed" preset hits: 3 cm across the face and 8 cm towards the toe.
Within about 2 cm across the face and 4.5 cm along it, ball speed drops by less than 6% and the direction changes by less than 10°.
Off-centre across the face, the bat twists in the hands and the ball flies off in the direction of the twist.
Miss the sweet spot and you often feel a sting in your hands. Some of the impact's energy has gone into shaking the bat instead of into the ball.
Their advice: build accurate timing first, then chase bat speed.
A ball hits 3 cm from the middle of the blade, across the face. What two things go wrong?
The ball comes off slower, and the bat twists in your hands (torque), sending the ball off line.

Hold a broom by the end of its handle and swing it. Then hold it near the brush and swing again. Same broom, same weight — but the first is much harder to swing. How hard something is to turn depends on its mass AND how far that mass is from where you turn it. Scientists call this the moment of inertia; players call it swing weight.

A heavier bat puts more mass behind the ball, but you can't swing it as fast. The slow-down is gentle: doubling the swing weight cuts swing speed by only about 16%. (Scientists say swing speed falls with the fourth root of the swing weight.)
The two effects nearly cancel. So across normal bat weights, the ball speed barely changes.
Choose the bat you can swing fastest and most accurately, not the heaviest you can lift.
Lab tests of cricket bats found knocking-in, English versus Kashmir willow and a composite back skin each changed performance by under 1.5%. That is small next to bat speed and timing.
Should you pick the heaviest bat you can lift?
No. The extra mass is almost cancelled out because you swing it slower. Pick the bat you can swing fastest and most accurately.
Where you hit matters almost as much as how.

Density is how much stuff is packed into a space. At sea level, a cubic metre of air — a big cupboard full — has a mass of about 1.2 kg. Warm air spreads out, so it is less dense. High up a mountain there is less air pressing down from above, so it is less dense there too. Less dense air pushes back less on a flying ball.

A spinning ball gets a push from the air, called the Magnus effect. Spin makes the air cling on longer on one side of the ball, so the air behind it is thrown the other way — and the ball is pushed the opposite way. Backspin, where the ball turns as if rolling backwards, pushes it UP.
Drag grows with the air's density, so thin air lets a hit carry further. At about 1,700 m — roughly Johannesburg's height above sea level — the air is nearly a fifth less dense than at sea level.
Mehta notes it's easier to hit a six on a hot day than on a cold night. The denser cold air slows the ball more.
A wind behind the batter carries the ball on. Hitting into it can be the difference between a six and a catch.
A clean lofted hit leaves the bat with backspin, which adds Magnus lift and carry. A knuckled hit with no backspin falls shorter.
Where would the same hit carry further: a cold night by the sea, or a hot afternoon in Johannesburg?
The hot afternoon in Johannesburg. Heat and height both make the air less dense, so there is less drag slowing the ball.
What the legs do, and how you train it.

Newton's third law: when you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard, the other way. Plant your front foot and push it towards the bowler, and the ground pushes back towards you. A firm front leg turns that push into a stop, so your hips turn instead of sliding forwards — like a door turning on its hinge.
Illustrative angles — the brace control is an estimate borrowed from baseball research, not a cricket measurement. The dashed line is a vertical through the front foot.
A firm front leg at impact gives the body something to turn around. Studies of baseball hitters found the front knee straightening into contact.
A higher backlift gives the bat a longer path to speed up, but costs time against fast bowling.

How you practise changes your technique. Against a bowling machine, batters leaned more on arms and wrists and used less hip–shoulder separation than against a real bowler. That is probably because the clues you see about the ball come later from a machine. Practise power hitting against real bowling when you can.
Brace and backlift are estimated controls in the simulator — plausible, but not measured in cricket.
Why does a collapsing front knee cost bat speed?
The hips slide on towards the bowler instead of turning around a firm post, so speed leaks away instead of passing up the chain.

A model is a simplified copy of the real world, built from rules. A map is a model: it leaves most things out so the important ones are clear. This simulator is only as good as its rules and the measurements behind them.

Two things that happen together don't always cause each other. Ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn — the sunny weather causes both. A study can show that a movement GOES WITH faster bats. That doesn't prove that copying it will make YOUR bat faster.
Bat speed comes from a regression on 20 male batters hitting straight back past a bowling machine. It shows which movements go with faster bats, not a recipe that works the same for everyone.
The body controls are linked in real life. You usually can't add 10° of separation without changing everything else.
Sequencing, brace and backlift effects are estimates from other sports.
The flight ignores fielders, gusts of wind and the ball running on after it lands.
Batters with more X-factor swing faster. Does that prove that adding X-factor will make your bat faster?
No. It shows the two go together in those 20 batters. Your body might need to change other things too, because the movements are linked.
Finger-spinner's stock ball: a mix of top-spin and side-spin, drifting away before turning in.
Seam angled 45° towards fine leg: the revs split evenly between top-spin (dip) and side-spin (turn).
Wrist-spinner's stock ball: more revs and more tilt — drifts in, then turns away.
Nearly all top-spin: dips hard, bounces steeply and goes straight on.
The wrist-spinner's wrong'un — out of the back of the hand, turning the other way to the leg-break.
The finger-spinner's wrong'un: an off-spinner's action that turns the ball away.
Flicked out with the middle finger: almost pure side-spin, so little dip but plenty of turn.
Back-spin: the Magnus force holds it up, it lands further on and skids through low.
The wrist-spinner's back-spinner, squeezed out from under the hand: floats, then hurries on.
Slower and higher: more time in the air for the spin to work.
Faster and flatter: less time for drift and dip.
Seam straight down the pitch: every rev goes into dip.
Seam facing the batter: every rev goes into turn off the pitch.
Let the seam tumble: less Magnus force, a little more drag.
20 km/h in the bowler's face: more airspeed, more drag, more dip.
20 km/h at the bowler's back: less airspeed, a flatter, longer ball.

Low friction, more bounce: the ball skids on.
About 1,700 m up on a warm day: thin air, less drag and less Magnus force.
A worn ball takes more Magnus lift than a new one.
A lacquered new ball takes the least Magnus lift.
Seam 20° to the slips, polished half towards the batter, ~120 km/h: starts on leg stump, swings away.
Seam 20° to fine leg: the same physics, mirrored — starts outside off and bends in.
The wind-tunnel sweet spot: 20° seam, 14 rev/s of backspin, about 108 km/h.
Old ball, rough half turned away from the seam, outswing grip at 140 km/h — it swings in.
The late inswinging yorker at the base of the stumps.
No tampering, no old ball: a new four-piece ball reverses on its own at extreme pace.
Seam bolt upright, rough half towards the batter, ~115 km/h: it swings towards the rough side.
Seam allowed to wobble: little swing, but it lands on the seam at unpredictable angles.
Released with almost no spin: no steady seam and no backspin lift, so it drops more.
A round-arm action tilts the backspin axis, so the Magnus force swings even a battered ball in — seam upright, no shine.
No quarter seams: stays smooth longer, so it holds conventional swing to far higher speeds.
20 km/h into the bowler's face raises the airspeed over the ball.
20 km/h at the bowler's back lowers the airspeed over the ball.
18 km/h across from the batter's off side changes the seam's angle to the air.
95 % humidity at the same temperature. Watch how little changes.
36 °C and dry: thinner air means less force — but warm air's higher viscosity also lowers the Reynolds number, keeping a quick ball out of reverse.
About 1,700 m up: thin air means less force — and a lower Reynolds number, so it takes more pace to reverse the ball.
18 rev/s: a steadier seam, but roughness starts to bite a little sooner.
All arms: little hip–shoulder separation, early release, a touch off-centre.
Good separation, a straightening front arm and a late wrist release.
Elite separation and sequencing, and it's middled.
The county hitter's swing — but 3 cm off-centre and low on the bat.
1.45 kg: more mass behind the ball, less swing speed.
1.05 kg: a quicker swing, less mass.

Five ideas you'll use in every card below.
You don't need to know any physics to use this lab. These five ideas are enough to start. Each card below adds one more idea, just before you need it.

Speed is how far something travels each second. Scientists measure it in metres per second (m/s). TV speed guns use kilometres per hour (km/h). To turn m/s into km/h, multiply by 3.6: 25 m/s is 90 km/h. Spin is counted in revolutions per minute (rpm) — how many full turns the ball makes in one minute.
A force is a push or a pull. We measure forces in newtons (N). One newton is about the weight of a small apple. A men's cricket ball weighs about 1.6 N.

Isaac Newton worked out two rules for how things move. First: a ball keeps going in a straight line at a steady speed unless a force acts on it. Second: when a force does act, the ball speeds up, slows down or changes direction. Scientists call any of these an acceleration. A bigger force gives a bigger acceleration.

Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth. Drop a ball and it falls about 5 m in the first second, getting faster all the way. A ball's weight is the pull of gravity on it. Every ball in this lab is falling like this while it flies — the other forces add to it.

Air resistance, or drag, is the air pushing back on anything that moves through it. Put your hand out of a moving bus window and you feel it. Drag always acts against the ball's motion, so it slows the ball down.
Spin adds one more force: a push from the air that can bend the ball down or sideways. Where that push comes from is the story of this lab.
A spinner lets the ball go at 25 m/s. How fast is that in km/h?
Every spinner's revs are a mix of three spins, and each does a different job.

Everything that spins turns around an imaginary line called its axis. A lattu (spinning top) spins around an upright axis. A wheel spins around its axle. The Earth spins around an axis through the North and South Poles. To describe a spin, say which way its axis points.
A spinner's axis can point in any direction. It helps to split that direction into three, measured against the line the ball is travelling along:
Top-spin — the axis lies across the pitch, so the ball rolls forwards like a bicycle wheel. The air pushes it down: dip.
Side-spin — the axis points along the line of flight, so the seam faces the batter. In the air there is almost no push at all. Its work starts when the ball lands and grips: turn.
Vertical-axis spin — the axis points straight up, like a lattu standing on the floor. The air pushes the ball sideways: drift.

A common mistake, even in serious write-ups, is to say side-spin makes the ball drift. Spin around the line of flight is lined up with the oncoming air. So at release, the air cannot push it sideways. Tap ▶ All side-spin and watch the yellow-orange arrow in the ball diagram vanish.
Real deliveries mix all three. The mix is what makes an off-break, a top-spinner and a carrom ball behave so differently from the same arm action.
Which kind of spin makes the ball dip, and which makes it turn off the pitch?
Top-spin (axis across the pitch) makes it dip. Side-spin (axis along the line of flight) makes it turn once it lands.
How a spinning ball pushes the air one way and gets pushed the other.

Look at a ceiling fan: dust stays stuck to the blades even though they spin fast. The air touching a surface gets dragged along with it, so it can't blow the dust off. A flying ball carries a thin skin of air like this, called the boundary layer. Round the back of the ball the layer lets go and leaves a swirly trail behind it: the wake.

Newton's third law: when you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard, the other way. Row a boat and you push water backwards, so the water pushes the boat forwards. Throw air one way and the air pushes you the other way.

Spin changes where the boundary layer lets go. On the side of the ball turning WITH the airflow, the layer hangs on longer. On the side turning INTO it, the layer breaks away sooner. So the wake is thrown out to one side. The ball has pushed the air that way, so the air pushes the ball the other way.

That push from the air on a spinning ball is called the Magnus effect, after the German scientist Gustav Magnus. It bends a football free kick, makes a top-spin table-tennis shot dip, and drifts a spinner's delivery.
How big is the push? Three more ideas, and then the formula scientists use.

Density is how much stuff is packed into a space. A bucket of water is far heavier than a bucket of air, because water is much denser. At sea level, a cubic metre of air — a big cupboard full — has a mass of about 1.2 kg. Denser air pushes harder on a ball.

Pushes from the air grow with the SQUARE of speed: speed × speed. Double the speed and the push is 2 × 2 = 4 times bigger. Triple it and the push is 3 × 3 = 9 times bigger. That's why a breeze barely moves you, but a storm can knock you over.

A coefficient is a number, found by measuring, that sums up how good something is at making a force. Two balls at the same speed can feel different pushes because of their surface or their spin. The coefficient holds that difference in one number, so one formula works for both.
Denser air, a bigger ball, a better-spinning ball and a faster ball all push harder. Speed counts twice: if C_L stays the same, a ball going twice as fast through the air feels four times the push.
F is the Magnus force in newtons. ρ (the Greek letter rho) is the air's density, A the area of the ball's shadow, v its speed through the air and C_L the lift coefficient.

S, the spin parameter, compares how fast the ball's surface spins with how fast the whole ball travels. At 1,800 rpm the surface moves at about 6.8 m/s. If the ball flies at 80 km/h (about 22 m/s), S is about 0.3.
R is the ball's radius and ω (the Greek letter omega) is how fast it turns, so R · ω is how fast a point on its surface moves. v is the ball's speed.

Wind-tunnel tests on real cricket balls (Keith, Britton & Liow, 2012) measured about 0.1–0.2 N of Magnus force at 17–28 m/s (about 60–100 km/h). That is a lift coefficient of roughly 0.10–0.14 — a push of roughly a tenth of the ball's weight.
They also found the push levels off above about 800 rpm. Spinning harder than that adds little extra Magnus force — though the extra revs still help the ball turn off the pitch.
Old balls took more Magnus force than new ones. And a new ball spun slowly (below about 800 rpm) could even have its push flip direction as its speed changed — the reverse Magnus effect.
The air rushes past a ball twice as fast, and its C_L doesn't change. How much bigger is the Magnus push?
Four times bigger. The push grows with speed squared, and 2 × 2 = 4.
Seam angle: sharing out the revs
Turn the seam and you move revs between dip and turn.

Where the seam points tells you how the revs are shared. With the seam rolling straight down the pitch, every rev is top-spin. Angle it towards fine leg (for a right-arm off-spinner) and some become side-spin. At 45° the split is exactly even.

Walk 10 steps diagonally across a courtyard, at 45°. You have gone about 7 steps forwards AND about 7 steps sideways. Why isn't that 10 in total? The two parts point at right angles, so they add by Pythagoras: 7.07² + 7.07² = 100 = 10². Any direction can be split into parts like this. Your calculator's cos and sin buttons give the two parts: cos 45° = sin 45° ≈ 0.71.

The shares are the cosine and sine of the seam angle. That's why they add up to more than 100%: the spin is being split into two directions, not cut like a pie. Check with Pythagoras: 71² + 71² is about 100².

The 45° ball makes the batter allow for dip AND turn at once. Robinson & Robinson (2016) found that swapping a little side-spin for top-spin, at the same revs, can land the ball up to 25 cm shorter. Its sideways drift hardly changes.
At a 60° seam angle, which job gets the bigger share of the revs: dip or turn?
Turn. The table gives 87% side-spin (turn) and only 50% top-spin (dip), because sin 60° ≈ 0.87 and cos 60° = 0.5.
Dip and drift aren't saved for the end — they grow with time squared.

When a steady push acts on a ball, the distance it moves doesn't grow steadily. It grows with time squared: distance = ½ × acceleration × time². After 1 second, call it 1 step. After 2 seconds it is 4 steps, and after 3 seconds 9 steps. The movement starts tiny and piles up at the end.

So halfway through the flight, a ball under a steady push has moved only a quarter of its final distance, because ½ × ½ = ¼. The other three-quarters arrive in the second half. To the batter, the ball seems to drop or swerve in the last few metres.

The ball also loses about a tenth of its speed to drag on the way, while its spin barely slows. So its spin parameter S creeps up. Because the Magnus force has already levelled off at spinners' revs, this helps only a little. The big extra helping is for side-spin.

A spinning object holds the direction of its axis. That's why a spinning lattu stays upright while a still one falls over, and why a spinning frisbee flies flat. A wheel spinning like this is called a gyroscope. A spun cricket ball does the same: its axis keeps pointing the way it did at release.

Gravity bends the ball's path downwards, but its spin axis keeps pointing where it did at release. So the axis and the oncoming air slowly move apart. Side-spin that was lined up with the air at release isn't lined up any more — and a sideways push grows through the delivery.

The simulator's "All side-spin" off-break. The spin axis (teal) keeps pointing where the ball was released, while the path (coral) bends down. The angle between them grows, and so does the sideways push. Height and sideways movement are stretched so you can see them.

That is why an off-break drifts away from a right-hander late, before turning back in off the pitch. The ball "generally drifts to the side opposite to which the ball will bounce" (Keith, Britton & Liow).
Tossing the ball up helps twice over. It gives more time for the time-squared effect, and a path that bends further from the spin axis.
Halfway to the batter, a ball has moved 10 cm sideways. If the push stays steady, how far has it moved by the end?
About 40 cm. Twice the time means 2 × 2 = 4 times the distance.
Why a dipping ball draws batters out of their crease.

A thrown ball moves forwards and falls at the same time. If you ignore the air, gravity only changes the up-and-down part: the ball falls just as a dropped ball would, while it carries on forwards. Together these make the familiar curved path. Years of catching teach your brain this curve, and it uses the curve to guess where a ball will land.

A batter has to start moving long before the ball arrives. So their feet go on a guess of where it will land. Top-spin adds a downward push on top of gravity, so the ball lands shorter — and sooner — than that guess.

A dipping ball also comes down more steeply. More of its speed is heading into the pitch, so it bounces higher than a flatter ball of the same pace. The batter who came forward to drive meets it higher on the bat than planned — or misses it.
Back-spin does the opposite. The Magnus force holds the ball up, so it lands further on than expected and arrives flatter, skidding through lower. That's the arm ball and the flipper.
Why does a top-spinner fool a batter who charges down the pitch to hit it on the full?
The top-spin adds a downward push to gravity. The ball lands shorter and sooner than the curve the batter's brain expected.
A seam that spins cleanly moves more in the air.

Watch the smoke from an incense stick. Near the tip it rises in a smooth, neat thread: laminar flow. Higher up it breaks into swirls and curls: turbulent flow. Air round a ball can flow either way. A bump like the seam can "trip" smooth air into churning, the way a stone in a stream makes the water tumble.
When the seam spins steadily around its axis, the air meets the same shape on every turn. The wake is thrown the same way every time — the steady conditions the Magnus force needs.
A scrambled seam tumbles instead. It trips the boundary layer into turbulence at random places all round the ball, so the push comes and goes.
Spinners sometimes scramble the seam on purpose, to hide a variation or to make the ball land unpredictably. The price is less movement through the air.

How much a scrambled seam costs has never been measured on cricket balls. The simulator uses a teaching estimate — a careful best guess, not a measurement. It takes up to about 45% off the Magnus force and adds a little drag.
Why does a scrambled seam move less in the air?
It trips the air into churning at random places, so the wake isn't thrown the same way each turn. The Magnus push keeps changing direction instead of adding up.
The air the ball flies through changes everything it does.

Cycle into the wind and the air rushes past you faster than you are riding. Cycle with the wind behind you and you barely feel a breeze. What the air does to a ball depends on its airspeed — how fast it moves compared with the AIR — not how fast it moves over the ground.
A headwind raises the ball's airspeed. Drag and the Magnus force both grow — roughly with the square of the airspeed — and the ball dips more. A tailwind does the opposite and carries it on.
A crosswind blows the ball sideways directly. In Robinson & Robinson's calculations, a light breeze moved a spinner's delivery further than its own spin drift did.

A crosswind also changes what side-spin does. It swings the oncoming air round, so spin that was lined up with the air isn't any more — and it becomes lift or dip. A breeze from the off side lifts an off-spinner's ball above the no-spin path. One from the leg side makes it dip below it.

Thin air means less of everything: less drag, less Magnus force, less drift and dip. Warm air spreads out, so on a hot day it is less dense. High up a mountain there is less air pressing down from above, so it is less dense there too.
Fun fact: the Earth's own spin (the Coriolis effect) nudges a flying ball too. For a slow bowler's delivery it is about a millimetre. You can safely ignore it.
A spinner bowls into a strong headwind. Will the ball dip more or less, and why?
More. The headwind raises the ball's speed through the air, and the Magnus push grows with that speed squared.
Off the pitch: grip, skid and bounce
Turn comes from friction — and friction has a limit.

Friction is the force that fights sliding. Rub your palms together and you can feel it. It has a limit: at most the grip number μ (the Greek letter mu) times how hard the two surfaces press together. Rubber soles on a dry floor have a high μ. Socks on a polished floor have a low one.

When the ball lands, its bottom slides across the pitch for a moment. Both its forward speed and its spin feed that slide. Side-spin rubs the bottom of the ball sideways, and friction pushes back the other way. That sideways shove is the turn.
Only spin that moves the bottom of the ball sideways can turn it. The turn figures are the simulator's default off-break on its two preset pitches.

Drop a ball on a hard floor. It bounces back up, but slower than it came down. The share of its downward speed it keeps is its restitution — a bounciness number. 0.5 means it leaves the ground at half the speed it hit it with. Hard pitches bounce more.
Friction can only push so hard: at most the pitch's grip (μ) times how hard the ball hits the ground. A steep, dipping ball lands harder, so it has more grip to work with.
More revs make the bottom of the ball slide sideways faster. More of the friction points sideways, so there is more turn.
A slower ball has less forward slide competing with the sideways slide, so it turns more too.
If friction is strong enough to stop the slide completely, the ball grips and leaves rolling. That is the "bite" of a dry pitch. On a damp or grassy one it skids on.
Grip and bounce are different properties. Friction decides the turn; restitution decides the bounce.
Spin around a vertical axis — the drift spin — only twists the bottom of the ball on the spot. It drifts the ball in the air but cannot turn it.
Same ball, same revs, two pitches: one dry and dusty, one damp and grassy. Which turns more, and which property of the pitch decides it?
The dry, dusty pitch. It has more friction (a higher μ), so it can push the ball sideways harder. Bounce (restitution) doesn't decide the turn.
Each variation is really just a different spin axis.
Now you know the three spins, you can read this table like a coach. Each variation is the same physics with the axis pointing a different way.
Drifts away from a right-hander, turns in
The same, spun the other way
Looks like a leg-break, turns in
Looks like an off-break, turns away
Holds up and skids on straight
The batter reads spin from the hand and the seam. A bowler who can change the axis without changing the action keeps them guessing every ball.
A googly and a leg-break come out of the same wrist-spinner's hand. What is actually different?
The spin axis. A googly is spun the other way — it is a wrist-spinner's off-break — so it turns in instead of away.
Every model simplifies. Here is how this one does.

A model is a simplified copy of the real world, built from rules. A map is a model: it leaves most things out so the important ones are clear. This simulator works out the forces on the ball and moves it on in tiny steps, a thousandth of a second at a time. It is only as good as its rules and the measurements behind them.
It leaves out swing from the seam at spinners' speeds, and the wobbly "knuckle" effect of a slowly tumbling seam.
It leaves out the reverse Magnus effect on a new ball spun slowly. Here the push always follows the spin.
Real pitches have cracks, footmarks and soft patches. This one is perfectly even.
Pitch friction and the scrambled-seam penalty are teaching estimates. The Magnus force, drag, air and bounce follow published measurements and textbook physics.
A real bowler's release is never the same twice.
The simulator says your off-break turns a few degrees. Why might a real ball, bowled the same way, turn a different amount?
Real pitches aren't even, pitch friction is only an estimate here, and no bowler releases the ball exactly the same way twice.

Speed is how far something travels each second. Scientists measure it in metres per second (m/s). TV speed guns use kilometres per hour (km/h). To turn m/s into km/h, multiply by 3.6: 30 m/s is 108 km/h. A swing bowler's backspin is counted in revolutions per second (rev/s) — full turns of the ball each second.

Isaac Newton worked out two rules for how things move. First: a ball keeps going in a straight line at a steady speed unless a force acts on it. Second: when a force does act, the ball speeds up, slows down or changes direction. Scientists call any of these an acceleration. A sideways force is what bends a ball off its straight line.

Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth. Drop a ball and it falls about 5 m in the first second. A ball's weight is the pull of gravity on it. We can compare any force with the ball's weight: "0.3 times the weight" means about a third as strong as gravity's pull.
Air resistance, or drag, is the air pushing back on anything that moves through it. Put your hand out of a moving bus window and you feel it. Drag acts against the ball's motion and slows it down.
Swing adds one more force: a sideways push from the air. It happens when the two halves of the ball treat the air differently. The cards below show how.
A seamer bowls at 36 m/s. Is that faster or slower than 130 km/h?
Swing is a tug-of-war between the two sides of the ball.

Watch the smoke from an incense stick. Near the tip it rises in a smooth, neat thread: laminar flow. Higher up it breaks into swirls and curls: turbulent flow. A boundary layer can be either. Churned-up air mixes in energy from the faster air outside it, so it can cling to a curved surface for longer.

Picture angles measured round the ball from the very front (0°) to the very back (180°). A smooth (laminar) layer lets go early, about 80° round. A churned-up (turbulent) layer hangs on to about 120°.

If one side lets go later than the other, the wake is thrown out towards the side that let go first. The ball has pushed the air that way, so the air pushes the ball the opposite way — towards the side where the air held on. Every kind of swing is a way of making that happen.
From above, the ball flying up the page. Dots mark where each half's boundary layer lets go; a wavy layer is turbulent. The angles come from the lab's swing simulator at 108, 151 and 115 km/h.
Pushes from the air grow with the SQUARE of speed: speed × speed. Double the speed and the push is 2 × 2 = 4 times bigger. That's why a breeze barely moves you, but a storm can knock you over.

A coefficient is a number, found by measuring, that sums up how good something is at making a force. A ball with a perfect seam and shine gets a bigger number than a battered one. The coefficient holds that difference, so one formula works for every ball.
Denser air, a bigger ball, a better ball and a faster ball all push harder. Speed counts twice: if C_S stays the same, twice the speed gives four times the sideways force.

F is the sideways force in newtons. ρ (the Greek letter rho) is the air's density, A the area of the ball's shadow, v its speed through the air and C_S the side-force coefficient. C_S reaches roughly 0.25–0.35 for a good new ball.

Whether a boundary layer stays smooth or churns up depends on one number: the Reynolds number (Re), named after the scientist Osborne Reynolds. It grows when the ball is faster or bigger. It shrinks when the fluid is stickier. Stickiness is called viscosity — honey is very viscous, water much less. Above a certain Reynolds number, the boundary layer churns up by itself.
Faster ball, bigger Reynolds number. A cricket ball at 30 m/s (108 km/h) has Re of about 1.4 × 10⁵. That means 140,000 — the "× 10⁵" in the readout means "times 100,000".

v is the ball's speed through the air, D its diameter and ν (the Greek letter nu) the air's stickiness. The Reynolds number decides whether a boundary layer is laminar or turbulent — which is why swing depends so heavily on pace.
One side of the ball's boundary layer lets go at 80°, the other at 120°. Which way is the ball pushed?
Towards the 120° side, where the air held on longer. The wake is thrown the other way, and the air pushes back.
The seam trips one side into turbulence.

Release the ball with the seam angled towards the slips, spinning backwards along the seam. On the seam's side, the boundary layer runs into the stitching and is tripped into turbulence — like a stone tripping a stream. On the other side it stays smooth (laminar), as long as that half is shiny. The turbulent side hangs on longer, so the ball swings the way the seam points.

Everything that spins turns around an imaginary line called its axis. A lattu (spinning top) spins around an upright axis; a wheel spins around its axle. A swing bowler spins the ball backwards around an axis straight across the seam, so the seam turns like a wheel.

A spinning object holds the direction of its axis. That's why a spinning lattu stays upright and a spinning frisbee flies flat. A wheel spinning like this is called a gyroscope. A swing bowler's backspin does the same for the seam: it stops the seam wobbling, so it trips the air on the same side all the way.
Best seam angle: about 20°. At lower speeds, a slightly more open seam trips the layer sooner.
Backspin keeps the seam steady. In wind-tunnel tests the side force grew with spin, up to about 11 revolutions a second.

Swing starts at around 15 m/s (55 km/h) and is strongest near 30 m/s (about 108 km/h). There the side force reached 0.3–0.4 times the ball's own weight — as if about a third of its weight were pulling it sideways.
The best balls were calculated — and photographed in real bowling — to move more than 80 cm by the time they reach the batter.
Keep the half away from the seam as smooth as possible. Conventional swing depends on that side staying laminar.
Why must the half AWAY from the seam be kept shiny for conventional swing?
That half must stay smooth (laminar), so its air lets go early. If it gets rough, its air churns up too, both sides hang on, and the swing fades.
At high speed the seam starts working against itself.

Golf balls have dimples for a reason. The little dents churn up the boundary layer, so it clings on longer and leaves a narrower wake — and a dimpled golf ball flies much further than a smooth one. A rough patch on a cricket ball works the same way: it churns up its air at a lower speed than a shiny patch would.

Bowl fast enough — push the Reynolds number high enough — and the boundary layer churns up on BOTH halves before it even reaches the seam. Now the seam does harm. It makes the turbulent layer on its own side thicker and weaker, so that layer lets go earlier than the untouched one opposite.
The push flips. The ball swings AWAY from where the seam points — an outswinger's grip that swings in.

Roughness brings the switch to lower speeds. R. D. Mehta measured a new four-piece ball reversing above about 36 m/s (roughly 130 km/h). A ball about 100 overs old reversed from about 30 m/s (108 km/h). A two-piece ball, with no quarter seams, reversed only above 45 m/s (162 km/h).
For reverse swing, the half away from the seam should be ROUGH — the opposite of conventional swing. Bowlers simply turn the ball over: same grip, same action.
No tampering is needed. Even a brand-new ball reverses, if you're quick enough.
Deliberately roughening the ball — with fingernails, bottle tops or the ground — is ball tampering, which the Laws forbid. Legal wear comes from normal play.
A bowler holds the ball for an outswinger, but at 140 km/h it swings IN. What has happened?
Reverse swing. At that speed both halves churn up before the seam, and the seam spoils its own side. So the ball swings away from where the seam points.

Once one half of the ball is rough and the other smooth, the seam isn't needed at all. Bowl it with the seam bolt upright. The rough half churns up (goes turbulent) at a lower speed than the smooth half. So it holds on longer, and the ball swings towards the rough side.
Bowl faster and both halves churn up. Now the layer over the rough half is thicker and lets go first — so the ball swings towards the smooth side.

Commentators often say a reversing ball "swings towards the shiny side". Mehta, who named contrast swing, points out that this is usually contrast swing, not true reverse swing. The speed at which it switches depends entirely on the state of both halves.
Because the seam is upright, it's the easiest swing to release. It even works with a battered, flattened seam. A seamer with a contrasting ball can swing it both ways just by turning it over.
In contrast swing at medium pace, does the ball swing towards the rough half or the shiny half?
Towards the rough half: its air churns up first and clings on longer. Only when it is bowled much faster does it switch to the shiny side.
About three-quarters of the swing happens in the second half of the flight.

When a steady push acts on a ball, the distance it moves doesn't grow steadily. It grows with time squared: after 1 second, call it 1 step; after 2 seconds, 4 steps; after 3 seconds, 9. Halfway through, the ball has moved only a quarter of the way (½ × ½ = ¼). The path this makes is a curve called a parabola.

Batters talk about a ball that "swung late" as if it waited. It didn't: the side force acts the whole way. Mehta's calculations, and photographs of a real swing bowler, show parabolic swing paths with about 75% of the movement in the second half of the flight.
The path hardly changes with speed, either. Between about 24 and 32 m/s (86–115 km/h) it looks almost the same. A faster ball feels a bigger force, but for less time.
What a batter sees as "late" is the ball bending most in the last few metres — exactly when there's no time left to adjust.
A ball swings 40 cm in total. Roughly how much of that happens in the second half of its flight?
About 30 cm — three-quarters of it — because sideways distance grows with time squared.
Wobble seam, knuckle ball and the sling
Other ways to move a ball through the air.

Spin makes the boundary layer hang on longer on one side of the ball than the other. The wake is thrown one way, so the ball is pushed the other: the Magnus effect. A swing bowler's backspin gives a small upward push that holds the ball up a little. The spin lab explains it in full.
Wobble seam — the seam is allowed to wobble. There is little steady swing, but the ball lands on the seam at unpredictable angles and can nip either way off the pitch.
Knuckle ball — released with almost no spin. Its seam drifts round during the flight, and the force goes with it. With no backspin to hold it up, it also drops sooner.
Sling-arm swing — a round-arm action tilts the backspin axis, so part of the Magnus force points sideways. Mehta showed this "Malinga swing" moves even an old ball with no shine and a flattened seam.
Seam movement — once the ball lands on its seam, it can jag off the pitch either way. That is seam bowling, and it isn't about the air at all.
The simulator models the wobble's lost swing, the knuckle ball's lost lift and the sling's tilted axis — but not the random seam movement off the pitch.
Why does a knuckle ball drop sooner than a normal delivery?
It has almost no backspin, so it loses the small upward Magnus push that holds a normal ball up.
Humid, overcast days — what actually changes?

Air is a crowd of tiny particles called molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. In humid air, some water-vapour molecules take the place of nitrogen and oxygen ones. A water molecule (H₂O) weighs 18 units, nitrogen (N₂) 28 and oxygen (O₂) 32. So damp air is LIGHTER than dry air. Warm air is lighter too: its molecules move faster and spread out, which is how a hot-air balloon floats.
Humidity: wind-tunnel tests, and tests firing balls through the air, found no increase in side force for humid or even wet balls. The seam didn't swell either.
Humid air is LIGHTER than dry air, not "heavy" — water vapour is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it replaces.
Temperature: air at 15 °C is about 4% denser than at 25 °C. By Mehta's estimate, a ball that swings 60 cm on a warm day swings only about 2.5 cm more on a cool one.
Cool air also nudges the Reynolds number up a few percent. That only matters for a ball that is already close to reversing.

Cloud cover: no firm evidence either way. One idea is that a new ball's shiny coating (lacquer) turns slightly tacky in damp air, giving more grip and more backspin — untested. Another is that bowlers simply concentrate on a cleaner release on "swinging days".
A soft, damp outfield does help, indirectly: the ball keeps its shine for longer.
Where the weather really matters is the wind — see the next card.
Your friend says the ball swings on humid days because damp air is heavier. What's wrong with that?
Damp air is actually lighter: water molecules (18) replace heavier nitrogen (28) and oxygen (32). And tests found humidity doesn't increase swing anyway.
The ball swings through the air — so the air's own movement matters.

Cycle into the wind and the air rushes past you faster than you are riding. Cycle with the wind behind you and you barely feel a breeze. What the air does to a ball depends on its airspeed — how fast it moves compared with the AIR. A side wind also changes the direction the air comes from, as the ball sees it.
A headwind raises the airspeed over the ball, and with it the Reynolds number. Bowling into the wind can tip a new ball into reverse swing, at a pace that would swing it normally in still air.
A tailwind lowers the airspeed. There is less force all round, and a quick bowler may drop back into conventional swing.
A crosswind changes the seam's angle to the oncoming air. A breeze from the off side closes an outswinger's seam angle by several degrees — and blows the ball towards leg as well.
Swing depends on the seam's angle to the AIR. That is one reason bowlers care which end they bowl from.
Left: the "Into a headwind" preset. Right: the "Breeze from off" outswinger, drawn to true angles — the breeze swings the oncoming air round and closes the seam's angle to it.
A new ball swings normally at 125 km/h in still air. Why might it reverse when bowled into a strong headwind?
The headwind makes the air rush past the ball faster. That raises its Reynolds number above the point where a new ball reverses — an airspeed of about 130 km/h.
The shine is a team job.
Polish only ONE half. Mehta's advice is to pick the half with the lighter embossment (the stamped lettering) and let the other roughen in play.
For conventional swing, keep the shiny half away from the seam. Once the other half is rough enough, turning the ball over sets up reverse swing — same grip, same action.
Only legal polishing counts. Check your competition's current rules on what you may use.
Why does the team polish only ONE half of the ball?
Conventional swing needs one half smooth, and the other half's roughness later makes reverse and contrast swing possible. Polish both halves and you lose the rough one.
The swing rules are tuned so the ball switches between kinds of swing at Mehta's measured speeds. Real balls vary a lot — even new balls of the same make.
It treats the seam's angle and wobble as steady. A real release is never perfect.
Seam movement off the pitch and gusts of wind are not included.
Wear is a teaching curve: "overs" stand in for how rough each half really is.
The simulator says your new ball reverses above about 130 km/h. Would every real new ball switch at exactly that speed?
No. Real balls vary a lot, even new ones of the same make, and no release is perfect. The simulator gives a typical value from Mehta's measurements.
